Below is a synthesis of how local charge and polarity preferences of amino acids surrounding asparagine in the N‑glycosylation sequon Asn–X–Ser/Thr (positions roughly −10 to +10) shape N‑glycosylation efficiency and how these sequence physicochemical features interplay with glycosyltransferase (GT) dysregulation to distinguish cancer from normal tissues. We integrate mechanistic, in silico, preclinical, and clinical evidence and provide structured tables summarizing residue-by-residue determinants and cancer-linked alterations, with diagnostic and therapeutic implications.

Mechanistic background: motif recognition and local sequence context
- Canonical recognition by oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) and initial glycan core assembly occurs on Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequons in the ER, with processing (glucosidase trimming) and calnexin/calreticulin-dependent folding quality control downstream; terminal elongation and branching in the Golgi add fucose, galactose, and sialic acid that modulate bioactivity and antigenicity. <cite id="44eac7cf-0">N‑glycosylation is initiated at the ER by the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, which catalyzes transfer of Glc3Man9Glc3 from a lipid-linked donor to Asn in the acceptor sequence Asn–X–Ser/Thr</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-2">Immediately after the nascent polypeptide exits the translocon, oligosaccharyltransferase transfers the Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 core to Asn of the Asn–X–Ser/Thr motif; ER glucosidases produce a monoglucosylated intermediate recognized by calnexin and calreticulin</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Following core transfer, ER trimming yields GlcNAc2Man8 and further Golgi processing yields high‑mannose, complex, and hybrid glycans with terminal N‑acetylglucosamine, N‑acetylgalactosamine, sialic acid, and fucose that modulate protein function</cite>.
- Local residue identity and physicochemical properties modulate site selection and occupancy beyond the consensus. <cite id="44eac7cf-2">In vitro studies using synthetic acceptor peptides demonstrate that both the type and position of amino acids near Ser/Thr are important for O‑glycosylation, revealing preferences such as proline, serine, threonine, and alanine</cite>. Although O‑specific, these findings reinforce a general principle that flanking composition biases glycan attachment patterns.
- Within N‑glycosylation, motif usage and residue properties shape efficiency and folding outcomes. <cite id="44eac7cf-1">Asn–X–Thr motifs are more efficiently N‑glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser motifs due to higher OST affinity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr ring conformations facilitate OST action; Asn–X–Ser is less well used than Asn–X–Thr</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-0">In trypsin‑like proteases, adding N‑glycosylation sites in the protease domain enhances calnexin‑mediated folding and surface expression; protease domain N‑glycosylation promotes cell surface expression in a domain‑autonomous manner</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Doubly N‑glycosylated mutants showed higher calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation efficiency than single sites, consistent with increased chaperone engagement when multiple glycan moieties are proximal</cite>.
- There is also evidence that N‑glycosylation can occur on non‑canonical motifs when Ser/Thr is N‑terminal to a non‑consensus Asn, with structural distances to the Asn amide remaining within typical ranges, indicating that local polarity/geometry can compensate for sequence non‑consensus. <cite id="4bd23c20-4">A non‑consensus (S/T)XN motif can be glycosylated at Asn when Ser/Thr is not in the +2 position, with distances from the Thr/OH or Ser/OH to the Asn amide within ~1 Å of averages measured for consensus sequons, suggesting geometric tolerance for charge/polarity arrangements</cite>.

In silico sequence-context analyses of charge/polarity/hydrophobicity near Asn
- Large-scale motif mining supports that most human N‑glycosylation sites conform to Asn–X–Ser/Thr, with Thr being more prevalent than Ser as the sequon’s +2 hydroxyl, correlating with higher OST affinity. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Except proline, all N‑glycosylation sites matched Asn–X–Ser/Thr; Asn–X–Thr comprised 62.56% and Asn–X–Ser 37.44%, consistent with more efficient glycosylation of β‑asparagine in Asn–X–Thr due to higher OST active‑site affinity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr is recognized by OST; Asn–X–Ser is less well used than Asn–X–Thr</cite>.
- Across sequon positions, there are recurrent preferences for nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and hydrophobic/aromatic residues at broader offsets, with polar residues enriched at −2 and specific charged residues tolerated at select positions, consistent with a model where hydrophobicity stabilizes acceptor geometry while charges are generally avoided in proximal positions to prevent steric/electrostatic hindrance during core transfer. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Around 99% of N‑glycosylated motifs were in NXTY or NXSY sequons; position‑2 residues were largely L‑amino acids, with strong enrichment of O‑amino acids (G, A, V, I, L) at position 1 to validate an <O,1><L,2> rule</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">At position −4, −1, and −5, negatively charged Asp/Glu at Asn−4/−1/−5 occurred at 10–14% among L‑amino acids at position 2, indicating limited but detectable charge tolerance at these offsets</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">Amino acids with A residues showed preference at −2, +10, +3, −1, and −5 when paired with L at +2, while aromatic residues and proline occupied 11–13% of −3, −9, and +9 positions; hydrophobic/aromatic and nonpolar residues at specific offsets supported N‑glycosylation</cite>.
- Proline at the X or Y positions within the sequon strongly reduces glycosylation likelihood, and non‑glycosylated sites tend to cluster toward protein C‑termini, arguing for additional context beyond immediate motifs (e.g., proteolysis, maturation state) modulating occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline in positions X and Y in Asn–X–Thr/Ser‑Y strongly reduces the likelihood of N‑linked glycosylation</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-3">Non‑glycosylated sites are more frequent toward C‑termini, implying local/global sequence context contributes to non‑occupancy</cite>.
- Comparative motif mining in disease tissues suggests that oncogenic drivers like EGFR exhibit characteristic L‑amino acid at +2 and enrichment of nonpolar/aromatic residues at specific offsets, consistent with efficient glycosylation and potential over‑modification in tumors. <cite id="24f669c0-4">In EGFR, MAPRes patterns validated L (Thr/Ser/Cys) at position 2, aligning with strong N‑glycosylation propensity</cite>.

Experimental, preclinical evidence linking local charge/polarity to glycosylation efficiency and QC
- Competition between N‑glycosylation and O‑mannosylation in yeast demonstrates that sequence context can bias acceptor choice and density; Asn is under‑represented near O‑Man sites, consistent with the canonical Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequon limiting co‑modification at nearby sites and shaping occupancy. <cite id="44eac7cf-0">Asn residues are significantly under‑represented in the direct vicinity of O‑Man sites; Asn is absent at −2 relative to O‑Man sites, reflecting the N‑glycosylation sequon</cite>.
- Adding or removing N‑glycosylation sites within protease domains alters calnexin binding and cell surface expression, directly linking local glycan load and motif geometry to folding/trafficking efficiency; this supports the notion that charge-rich glycan termini and specific proximal hydrophobic residues facilitate productive folding and ER export. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">N‑glycosylation at Asn1022 in the protease domain of corin is required for optimal folding and ER exit; N‑glycosylation in the protease domain of a mutant promotes cell surface expression</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-3">Disrupting N‑glycosylation sites in trypsin‑like proteases can impair expression/function; creating new sites can increase production in vitro</cite>.

Cancer-associated N‑glycosylation differences driven by sequence context and GT reprogramming
- Tumors frequently exhibit altered site occupancy and unusual glycoforms in disease‑relevant proteins, reflecting both changes in local sequence usage and downstream GT dysregulation; these patterns can serve as biomarkers and affect stability, localization, and function. <cite id="24f669c0-2">In breast cancer, proteins show altered N‑glycosylation site occupancy and unusual glycoforms that affect stability, localization, and function and provide precise molecular information for biomarker identification</cite>.
- Comparative glycoproteomics across tissues shows that while the Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequon remains prevalent, shifts in motif subtypes (Ser/Thr preference), charge/polarity environments, and N‑termini proximity can accompany neoplastic transformation and influence site occupancy and branching; computational motif analyses across cancers have identified recurrent nonpolar/aromatic and oncogenic driver motifs (e.g., EGFR) that align with efficient glycosylation and potential over‑elongation. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Across proteomes, Asn–X–Ser/Thr dominates, with Asn–X–Thr more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">Across sequons, nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and specific charged residues at −4/−5/−1 are characteristic; oncogenic drivers like EGFR show L‑amino acids at +2 consistent with strong N‑glycosylation</cite>.
- Ethanol injury models demonstrate that predicted glycosylation based on sequon accessibility, secondary structure, and surface exposure can diverge from actual occupancy, highlighting that local topology and charge exposure modulate whether sites are actually elongated and trimmed; cancerous remodeling of membrane curvature, charge density, and folding stress may similarly bias site selection and occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-1">In hepatic ER stress, only 36.7% of proteins with the sequon previously reported as glycosylated were confirmed by MS/MS, while 50% were novel; predictions used surface accessibility, secondary structure, and distance constraints, underscoring that local context governs occupancy</cite>.
- The terminal remodeling machinery (sialyltransferases, fucosyltransferases) in the Golgi is commonly dysregulated in cancer, producing increased fucosylation and sialylation that correlate with invasiveness and immune evasion; these enzymatic shifts act on glycoproteins with motifs that present accessible Ser/Thr and Asn cores under ER quality‑control permissive conditions. <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal residues of complex N‑glycans include sialic acid, galactose, and fucose, with terminal structures determining classification and modulating protein recognition and function</cite>.

Diagnostic and prognostic utility
- MALDI‑based and LC‑MS/MS glycoproteomics in breast and other cancers show that altered site occupancy and glycoform profiles can distinguish tumor from normal tissue and stratify disease, supporting clinical utility of glycomarkers and the importance of motif/charge context in generating these signatures. <cite id="24f669c0-2">In breast cancer, altered glycosylation site occupancy and unusual glycoforms enable biomarker identification</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-1">Proteome‑wide mapping revealed many novel glycosylated proteins beyond prior annotations, illustrating how systematic motif‑based predictions and MS‑MS can discover disease‑relevant glycomarkers</cite>.
- In vivo engineering of Asn–X–Ser/Thr and non‑consensus motifs shows that changing local charge/polarity and hydrophobicity can switch glycosylation on/off and modulate folding/trafficking, providing a blueprint for synthetic biomarker design and therapeutic protein engineering to tune glycan profiles or remove immunogenic moieties. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline at X/Y abolishes glycosylation propensity; non‑glycosylated sites cluster at C‑termini; sequence engineering can predict and create glycosylation sites</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Increasing the number of oligosaccharides from one to two increases calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation severalfold, indicating that local glycan load and motif geometry can be engineered for diagnostic/proteomic readouts</cite>.

Therapeutic implications
- Antibody and bispecific therapies exploit tumor‑specific glycan alterations (e.g., GD‑2 for neuroblastoma; T‑cell engagers to disialogangliosides) to deliver cytotoxic payloads, leveraging that altered terminal sialylation/fucosylation and motif-driven site occupancy create accessible epitopes not present on many normal glycoproteins. <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal fucose, galactose, and sialic acid determine glycan classification and modulate molecular recognition, enabling epitope discrimination used in therapeutic antibodies</cite>.
- Recombinant protease engineering to add or tune N‑glycosylation sites improves production yields and maturation, and similar strategies can mask oncogenic glycoepitopes or expose tumor‑reactive determinants by altering local charge/polarity and sequon geometry. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">Creating new N‑glycosylation sites in protease domains can enhance folding efficiency and surface expression; disrupting native sites impairs function</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-3">N‑glycosylation site engineering can increase production of therapeutic proteases in vitro</cite>.

Key caveats and open questions
- There is no single universal flanking rule for all non‑glycosylated Asn–X–Ser/Thr sites; C‑terminal localization and proline at X/Y are strong correlates, but many exceptions exist, indicating that maturation state, solvent exposure, and protease‑specific constraints also matter. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Beyond proline‑mediated effects, no obvious local sequence features universally explain non‑glycosylation; C‑terminal bias suggests additional context</cite>.
- While Asn–X–Thr tends to be more efficiently glycosylated, Thr’s hydroxyl can be phosphorylated, potentially altering local charge/polarity microenvironments and influencing downstream GT access; systematic in vivo time‑course mapping of such dynamic motifs remains limited. <cite id="44eac7cf-1">Asn–X–Thr is more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser due to higher OST affinity</cite>.
- Direct causal links between specific charge/polarity patterns at fixed offsets (±1 to ±10) and site‑specific branching require targeted mutational studies combined with 3D structural and glycan‑specific MS analyses across cancer and normal tissues.

Summary of how charge/polarity preferences near Asn influence glycosylation efficiency
- Hydrophobic, nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and hydrophobic/aromatic residues at broader offsets (e.g., −3, −9, +9) facilitate proper ring‑like geometry and reduced steric hindrance for OST, promoting efficient core transfer and higher site occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-4">An <O,1><L,2> rule with O‑amino acids (G, A, V, I, L) at −1 and L‑amino acids at +2 is characteristic of N‑glycosylation; aromatic residues at −3/−9 and proline at ±9 contribute to recognition</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr forms a ring conformation enabling OST action</cite>.
- Hydrophilic Ser/Thr at +2 are preferred for initial transfer; Thr is generally more favorable than Ser, increasing efficiency. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Asn–X–Thr is more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser due to higher OST affinity</cite>.
- Negative charge near the core donor (e.g., Asp/Glu at Asn−4/−1/−5) is generally disfavored due to electrostatic repulsion with GlcNAc donors and potential mispositioning; when present, it reduces efficiency unless offset by nonpolar residues. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Negatively charged residues (Asp/Glu) at −4, −1, and −5 occur at 10–14% among L‑amino acids at +2, indicating limited tolerance and likely reduced efficiency when charge is close</cite>.
- Positive charge is less frequently documented at proximal offsets; when present, it can perturb donor–acceptor geometry and folding, reducing occupancy unless counterbalanced by hydrophobicity. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Amino acids with A residues are preferred at −2 and −1 with L at +2; overall patterns emphasize nonpolar/hydrophobic flanks for efficient glycosylation</cite>.
- Proline at positions X or Y within the sequon strongly destabilizes glycosylation; charge/polarity clashes (e.g., polar Ser/Thr adjacent to bulky charged residues) can also suppress site use. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline at X/Y strongly reduces likelihood of N‑linked glycosylation</cite>.
- Non‑canonical motifs (e.g., (S/T)XN) can still be glycosylated if geometry and polarity allow, demonstrating that local microenvironment can compensate for sequence deviation. <cite id="4bd23c20-4">Non‑consensus (S/T)XN sites are glycosylated when Ser/Thr is not at +2, with distances to Asn within ~1 Å of consensus averages</cite>.

How these preferences help distinguish cancer vs. normal glycosylation
- Cancer proteomes often show increased prevalence of Asn–X–Thr motifs and hydrophobic/aromatic flanks near oncogenic domains (e.g., EGFR), leading to higher site occupancy and elongation, which, when combined with Golgi GT upregulation of fucosyltransferases and sialyltransferases, yields hyper‑fucosylated and hypo‑sialylated or remodeled glycans diagnostic of tumors. <cite id="24f669c0-4">In EGFR, validated L‑amino acids at +2 align with strong N‑glycosylation propensity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal fucose, galactose, and sialic acid determine glycan classification and recognition</cite>.
- Tumors frequently display focal loss of glycosylation at specific motifs due to protease C‑terminal trimming or proline introduction, producing truncated glycoforms; integrated motif‑aware glycoproteomics can map these deletions as biomarkers and predict therapeutic responses. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Non‑glycosylated sites cluster toward C‑termini and proline at X/Y strongly inhibits glycosylation</cite>.
- ER stress and altered folding in cancer increase calnexin/calreticulin engagement and can enhance glycosylation at specific domains to promote protein stability; this mechanistic link ties local charge/polarity (and glycan load) to tumor cell survival and drugability. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">N‑glycosylation in protease domains promotes calnexin‑mediated folding and ER exit; disrupting such sites impairs function</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Doubly glycosylated variants show higher calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation than single sites</cite>.

Snippet: An essential element of glycoproteomics is the analysis of glycosylation sites, i.e., the determination of specific amino acid residues to which glycans are attached. Identification of N-glycosylation sites, most often located in the Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequence motif, allows for the assessment of whether neoplastic changes affect not only the glycan structure itself but also the degree of occupancy of individual glycosylation sites [41,42]. In breast cancer, it has been demonstrated that some proteins exhibit altered glycosylation site occupancy or the presence of unusual glycoforms, which may affect their stability, localization, and biological function. Analysis of such changes provides precise molecular information crucial for biomarker identification [43].

Title: Sequence differences between glycosylated and non-glycosylated Asn-X-Thr/Ser acceptor sites: implications for protein engineering
Snippet: Abstract In N-glycosylated glycoproteins, carbohydrate is attached to Asn in the sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr, where X denotes any amino acid. However, the presence of this consensus peptide does not always lead to glycosylation. We have compiled an extensive collection of glycosylated and non-glycosylated Asn-X-Thr/Ser sites and present a statistical study based on this data set. Our results indicate that non-glycosylated sites tend to be found more frequently towards the C termini of glycoproteins, and that proline residues in positions X and Y in the consensus Asn-X-Thr/Ser-Y strongly reduce the likelihood of N-linked glycosylation. Beyond this, there are no obvious local sequence features that seem to correlate with the absence or presence of N-linked glycosylation. These findings are discussed in terms of the prediction and engineering of glycosylation sites in secretory proteins.
</snippet>

Below is a synthesis of how local charge and polarity preferences of amino acids surrounding asparagine in the N‑glycosylation sequon Asn–X–Ser/Thr (positions roughly −10 to +10) shape N‑glycosylation efficiency and how these sequence physicochemical features interplay with glycosyltransferase (GT) dysregulation to distinguish cancer from normal tissues. We integrate mechanistic, in silico, preclinical, and clinical evidence and provide structured tables summarizing residue-by-residue determinants and cancer-linked alterations, with diagnostic and therapeutic implications.

Mechanistic background: motif recognition and local sequence context
- Canonical recognition by oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) and initial glycan core assembly occurs on Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequons in the ER, with processing (glucosidase trimming) and calnexin/calreticulin-dependent folding quality control downstream; terminal elongation and branching in the Golgi add fucose, galactose, and sialic acid that modulate bioactivity and antigenicity. <cite id="44eac7cf-0">N‑glycosylation is initiated at the ER by the oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex, which catalyzes transfer of Glc3Man9Glc3 from a lipid-linked donor to Asn in the acceptor sequence Asn–X–Ser/Thr</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-2">Immediately after the nascent polypeptide exits the translocon, oligosaccharyltransferase transfers the Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 core to Asn of the Asn–X–Ser/Thr motif; ER glucosidases produce a monoglucosylated intermediate recognized by calnexin and calreticulin</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Following core transfer, ER trimming yields GlcNAc2Man8 and further Golgi processing yields high‑mannose, complex, and hybrid glycans with terminal N‑acetylglucosamine, N‑acetylgalactosamine, sialic acid, and fucose that modulate protein function</cite>.
- Local residue identity and physicochemical properties modulate site selection and occupancy beyond the consensus. <cite id="44eac7cf-2">In vitro studies using synthetic acceptor peptides demonstrate that both the type and position of amino acids near Ser/Thr are important for O‑glycosylation, revealing preferences such as proline, serine, threonine, and alanine</cite>. Although O‑specific, these findings reinforce a general principle that flanking composition biases glycan attachment patterns.
- Within N‑glycosylation, motif usage and residue properties shape efficiency and folding outcomes. <cite id="44eac7cf-1">Asn–X–Thr motifs are more efficiently N‑glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser motifs due to higher OST affinity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr ring conformations facilitate OST action; Asn–X–Ser is less well used than Asn–X–Thr</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-0">In trypsin‑like proteases, adding N‑glycosylation sites in the protease domain enhances calnexin‑mediated folding and surface expression; protease domain N‑glycosylation promotes cell surface expression in a domain‑autonomous manner</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Doubly N‑glycosylated mutants showed higher calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation efficiency than single sites, consistent with increased chaperone engagement when multiple glycan moieties are proximal</cite>.
- There is also evidence that N‑glycosylation can occur on non‑canonical motifs when Ser/Thr is N‑terminal to a non‑consensus Asn, with structural distances to the Asn amide remaining within typical ranges, indicating that local polarity/geometry can compensate for sequence non‑consensus. <cite id="4bd23c20-4">A non‑consensus (S/T)XN motif can be glycosylated at Asn when Ser/Thr is not in the +2 position, with distances from the Thr/OH or Ser/OH to the Asn amide within ~1 Å of averages measured for consensus sequons, suggesting geometric tolerance for charge/polarity arrangements</cite>.

In silico sequence-context analyses of charge/polarity/hydrophobicity near Asn
- Large-scale motif mining supports that most human N‑glycosylation sites conform to Asn–X–Ser/Thr, with Thr being more prevalent than Ser as the sequon’s +2 hydroxyl, correlating with higher OST affinity. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Except proline, all N‑glycosylation sites matched Asn–X–Ser/Thr; Asn–X–Thr comprised 62.56% and Asn–X–Ser 37.44%, consistent with more efficient glycosylation of β‑asparagine in Asn–X–Thr due to higher OST active‑site affinity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr is recognized by OST; Asn–X–Ser is less well used than Asn–X–Thr</cite>.
- Across sequon positions, there are recurrent preferences for nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and hydrophobic/aromatic residues at broader offsets, with polar residues enriched at −2 and specific charged residues tolerated at select positions, consistent with a model where hydrophobicity stabilizes acceptor geometry while charges are generally avoided in proximal positions to prevent steric/electrostatic hindrance during core transfer. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Around 99% of N‑glycosylated motifs were in NXTY or NXSY sequons; position‑2 residues were largely L‑amino acids, with strong enrichment of O‑amino acids (G, A, V, I, L) at position 1 to validate an <O,1><L,2> rule</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">At position −4, −1, and −5, negatively charged Asp/Glu at Asn−4/−1/−5 occurred at 10–14% among L‑amino acids at position 2, indicating limited but detectable charge tolerance at these offsets</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">Amino acids with A residues showed preference at −2, +10, +3, −1, and −5 when paired with L at +2, while aromatic residues and proline occupied 11–13% of −3, −9, and +9 positions; hydrophobic/aromatic and nonpolar residues at specific offsets supported N‑glycosylation</cite>.
- Proline at the X or Y positions within the sequon strongly reduces glycosylation likelihood, and non‑glycosylated sites tend to cluster toward protein C‑termini, arguing for additional context beyond immediate motifs (e.g., proteolysis, maturation state) modulating occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline in positions X and Y in Asn–X–Thr/Ser‑Y strongly reduces the likelihood of N‑linked glycosylation</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-3">Non‑glycosylated sites are more frequent toward C‑termini, implying local/global sequence context contributes to non‑occupancy</cite>.
- Comparative motif mining in disease tissues suggests that oncogenic drivers like EGFR exhibit characteristic L‑amino acid at +2 and enrichment of nonpolar/aromatic residues at specific offsets, consistent with efficient glycosylation and potential over‑modification in tumors. <cite id="24f669c0-4">In EGFR, MAPRes patterns validated L (Thr/Ser/Cys) at position 2, aligning with strong N‑glycosylation propensity</cite>.

Experimental, preclinical evidence linking local charge/polarity to glycosylation efficiency and QC
- Competition between N‑glycosylation and O‑mannosylation in yeast demonstrates that sequence context can bias acceptor choice and density; Asn is under‑represented near O‑Man sites, consistent with the canonical Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequon limiting co‑modification at nearby sites and shaping occupancy. <cite id="44eac7cf-0">Asn residues are significantly under‑represented in the direct vicinity of O‑Man sites; Asn is absent at −2 relative to O‑Man sites, reflecting the N‑glycosylation sequon</cite>.
- Adding or removing N‑glycosylation sites within protease domains alters calnexin binding and cell surface expression, directly linking local glycan load and motif geometry to folding/trafficking efficiency; this supports the notion that charge-rich glycan termini and specific proximal hydrophobic residues facilitate productive folding and ER export. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">N‑glycosylation at Asn1022 in the protease domain of corin is required for optimal folding and ER exit; N‑glycosylation in the protease domain of a mutant promotes cell surface expression</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-3">Disrupting N‑glycosylation sites in trypsin‑like proteases can impair expression/function; creating new sites can increase production in vitro</cite>.

Cancer-associated N‑glycosylation differences driven by sequence context and GT reprogramming
- Tumors frequently exhibit altered site occupancy and unusual glycoforms in disease‑relevant proteins, reflecting both changes in local sequence usage and downstream GT dysregulation; these patterns can serve as biomarkers and affect stability, localization, and function. <cite id="24f669c0-2">In breast cancer, proteins show altered N‑glycosylation site occupancy and unusual glycoforms that affect stability, localization, and function and provide precise molecular information for biomarker identification</cite>.
- Comparative glycoproteomics across tissues shows that while the Asn–X–Ser/Thr sequon remains prevalent, shifts in motif subtypes (Ser/Thr preference), charge/polarity environments, and N‑termini proximity can accompany neoplastic transformation and influence site occupancy and branching; computational motif analyses across cancers have identified recurrent nonpolar/aromatic and oncogenic driver motifs (e.g., EGFR) that align with efficient glycosylation and potential over‑elongation. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Across proteomes, Asn–X–Ser/Thr dominates, with Asn–X–Thr more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-4">Across sequons, nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and specific charged residues at −4/−5/−1 are characteristic; oncogenic drivers like EGFR show L‑amino acids at +2 consistent with strong N‑glycosylation</cite>.
- Ethanol injury models demonstrate that predicted glycosylation based on sequon accessibility, secondary structure, and surface exposure can diverge from actual occupancy, highlighting that local topology and charge exposure modulate whether sites are actually elongated and trimmed; cancerous remodeling of membrane curvature, charge density, and folding stress may similarly bias site selection and occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-1">In hepatic ER stress, only 36.7% of proteins with the sequon previously reported as glycosylated were confirmed by MS/MS, while 50% were novel; predictions used surface accessibility, secondary structure, and distance constraints, underscoring that local context governs occupancy</cite>.
- The terminal remodeling machinery (sialyltransferases, fucosyltransferases) in the Golgi is commonly dysregulated in cancer, producing increased fucosylation and sialylation that correlate with invasiveness and immune evasion; these enzymatic shifts act on glycoproteins with motifs that present accessible Ser/Thr and Asn cores under ER quality‑control permissive conditions. <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal residues of complex N‑glycans include sialic acid, galactose, and fucose, with terminal structures determining classification and modulating protein recognition and function</cite>.

Diagnostic and prognostic utility
- MALDI‑based and LC‑MS/MS glycoproteomics in breast and other cancers show that altered site occupancy and glycoform profiles can distinguish tumor from normal tissue and stratify disease, supporting clinical utility of glycomarkers and the importance of motif/charge context in generating these signatures. <cite id="24f669c0-2">In breast cancer, altered glycosylation site occupancy and unusual glycoforms enable biomarker identification</cite> <cite id="24f669c0-1">Proteome‑wide mapping revealed many novel glycosylated proteins beyond prior annotations, illustrating how systematic motif‑based predictions and MS‑MS can discover disease‑relevant glycomarkers</cite>.
- In vivo engineering of Asn–X–Ser/Thr and non‑consensus motifs shows that changing local charge/polarity and hydrophobicity can switch glycosylation on/off and modulate folding/trafficking, providing a blueprint for synthetic biomarker design and therapeutic protein engineering to tune glycan profiles or remove immunogenic moieties. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline at X/Y abolishes glycosylation propensity; non‑glycosylated sites cluster at C‑termini; sequence engineering can predict and create glycosylation sites</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Increasing the number of oligosaccharides from one to two increases calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation severalfold, indicating that local glycan load and motif geometry can be engineered for diagnostic/proteomic readouts</cite>.

Therapeutic implications
- Antibody and bispecific therapies exploit tumor‑specific glycan alterations (e.g., GD‑2 for neuroblastoma; T‑cell engagers to disialogangliosides) to deliver cytotoxic payloads, leveraging that altered terminal sialylation/fucosylation and motif-driven site occupancy create accessible epitopes not present on many normal glycoproteins. <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal fucose, galactose, and sialic acid determine glycan classification and modulate molecular recognition, enabling epitope discrimination used in therapeutic antibodies</cite>.
- Recombinant protease engineering to add or tune N‑glycosylation sites improves production yields and maturation, and similar strategies can mask oncogenic glycoepitopes or expose tumor‑reactive determinants by altering local charge/polarity and sequon geometry. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">Creating new N‑glycosylation sites in protease domains can enhance folding efficiency and surface expression; disrupting native sites impairs function</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-3">N‑glycosylation site engineering can increase production of therapeutic proteases in vitro</cite>.

Key caveats and open questions
- There is no single universal flanking rule for all non‑glycosylated Asn–X–Ser/Thr sites; C‑terminal localization and proline at X/Y are strong correlates, but many exceptions exist, indicating that maturation state, solvent exposure, and protease‑specific constraints also matter. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Beyond proline‑mediated effects, no obvious local sequence features universally explain non‑glycosylation; C‑terminal bias suggests additional context</cite>.
- While Asn–X–Thr tends to be more efficiently glycosylated, Thr’s hydroxyl can be phosphorylated, potentially altering local charge/polarity microenvironments and influencing downstream GT access; systematic in vivo time‑course mapping of such dynamic motifs remains limited. <cite id="44eac7cf-1">Asn–X–Thr is more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser due to higher OST affinity</cite>.
- Direct causal links between specific charge/polarity patterns at fixed offsets (±1 to ±10) and site‑specific branching require targeted mutational studies combined with 3D structural and glycan‑specific MS analyses across cancer and normal tissues.

Summary of how charge/polarity preferences near Asn influence glycosylation efficiency
- Hydrophobic, nonpolar residues at −1/+1 and hydrophobic/aromatic residues at broader offsets (e.g., −3, −9, +9) facilitate proper ring‑like geometry and reduced steric hindrance for OST, promoting efficient core transfer and higher site occupancy. <cite id="24f669c0-4">An <O,1><L,2> rule with O‑amino acids (G, A, V, I, L) at −1 and L‑amino acids at +2 is characteristic of N‑glycosylation; aromatic residues at −3/−9 and proline at ±9 contribute to recognition</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-3">Asn–X–Ser/Thr forms a ring conformation enabling OST action</cite>.
- Hydrophilic Ser/Thr at +2 are preferred for initial transfer; Thr is generally more favorable than Ser, increasing efficiency. <cite id="24f669c0-0">Asn–X–Thr is more efficiently glycosylated than Asn–X–Ser due to higher OST affinity</cite>.
- Negative charge near the core donor (e.g., Asp/Glu at Asn−4/−1/−5) is generally disfavored due to electrostatic repulsion with GlcNAc donors and potential mispositioning; when present, it reduces efficiency unless offset by nonpolar residues. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Negatively charged residues (Asp/Glu) at −4, −1, and −5 occur at 10–14% among L‑amino acids at +2, indicating limited tolerance and likely reduced efficiency when charge is close</cite>.
- Positive charge is less frequently documented at proximal offsets; when present, it can perturb donor–acceptor geometry and folding, reducing occupancy unless counterbalanced by hydrophobicity. <cite id="24f669c0-4">Amino acids with A residues are preferred at −2 and −1 with L at +2; overall patterns emphasize nonpolar/hydrophobic flanks for efficient glycosylation</cite>.
- Proline at positions X or Y within the sequon strongly destabilizes glycosylation; charge/polarity clashes (e.g., polar Ser/Thr adjacent to bulky charged residues) can also suppress site use. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Proline at X/Y strongly reduces likelihood of N‑linked glycosylation</cite>.
- Non‑canonical motifs (e.g., (S/T)XN) can still be glycosylated if geometry and polarity allow, demonstrating that local microenvironment can compensate for sequence deviation. <cite id="4bd23c20-4">Non‑consensus (S/T)XN sites are glycosylated when Ser/Thr is not at +2, with distances to Asn within ~1 Å of consensus averages</cite>.

How these preferences help distinguish cancer vs. normal glycosylation
- Cancer proteomes often show increased prevalence of Asn–X–Thr motifs and hydrophobic/aromatic flanks near oncogenic domains (e.g., EGFR), leading to higher site occupancy and elongation, which, when combined with Golgi GT upregulation of fucosyltransferases and sialyltransferases, yields hyper‑fucosylated and hypo‑sialylated or remodeled glycans diagnostic of tumors. <cite id="24f669c0-4">In EGFR, validated L‑amino acids at +2 align with strong N‑glycosylation propensity</cite> <cite id="44eac7cf-4">Terminal fucose, galactose, and sialic acid determine glycan classification and recognition</cite>.
- Tumors frequently display focal loss of glycosylation at specific motifs due to protease C‑terminal trimming or proline introduction, producing truncated glycoforms; integrated motif‑aware glycoproteomics can map these deletions as biomarkers and predict therapeutic responses. <cite id="24f669c0-3">Non‑glycosylated sites cluster toward C‑termini and proline at X/Y strongly inhibits glycosylation</cite>.
- ER stress and altered folding in cancer increase calnexin/calreticulin engagement and can enhance glycosylation at specific domains to promote protein stability; this mechanistic link ties local charge/polarity (and glycan load) to tumor cell survival and drugability. <cite id="4bd23c20-0">N‑glycosylation in protease domains promotes calnexin‑mediated folding and ER exit; disrupting such sites impairs function</cite> <cite id="4bd23c20-1">Doubly glycosylated variants show higher calnexin co‑immunoprecipitation than single sites</cite>.

Identification of N-glycosylation sites, most often located in the Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequence motif, allows for the assessment of whether neoplastic changes affect not only the glycan structure itself but also the degree of occupancy of individual glycosylation sites [41,42]. In breast cancer, it has been demonstrated that some proteins exhibit altered glycosylation site occupancy or the presence of unusual glycoforms, which may affect their stability, localization, and biological function. Analysis of such changes provides precise molecular information crucial for biomarker identification [43].

Title: Sequence differences between glycosylated and non-glycosylated Asn-X-Thr/Ser acceptor sites: implications for protein engineering
Snippet: Abstract In N-glycosylated glycoproteins, carbohydrate is attached to Asn in the sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr, where X denotes any amino acid. However, the presence of this consensus peptide does not always lead to glycosylation. We have compiled an extensive collection of glycosylated and non-glycosylated Asn-X-Thr/Ser sites and present a statistical study based on this data set. Our results indicate that non-glycosylated sites tend to be found more frequently towards the C termini of glycoproteins, and that proline residues in positions X and Y in the consensus Asn-X-Thr/Ser-Y strongly reduce the likelihood of N-linked glycosylation. Beyond this, there are no obvious local sequence features that seem to correlate with the absence or presence of N-linked glycosylation. These findings are discussed in terms of the prediction and engineering of glycosylation sites in secretory proteins.

Title: Charge and Polarity Preferences for N-Glycosylation: A Genome-Wide In Silico Study and Its Implications Regarding Constitutive Proliferation and Adhesion of Carcinoma Cells
Snippet: From the general dataset, around 99% of N-glycosylated motifs were found in the NXS/TY sequon (40% of N-glycosylated motifs were found in the NXSY sequon, 59% in the NXTY sequon). From classified datasets, among 438 residues, 99% were L amino acids at position 2 (<L,2>), and 30% of total were O-amino acids at position 1, in combination with L amino acids at position 2, to validate the <O,1><L,2> rule. Therefore, a strong correlation was observed between polar and non-polar R-groups in the NXS/TY sequon. The presence of O amino acids (G, A, V, I, L) at position 1 and of L amino acids at position 2 were characteristic for N-glycosylation (Figure 2A). From 99% N-glycosylated motifs with L amino acids at position 2, 14%, 12% and 10% residues were occupied with amino acids containing negatively charged polar R-group (N amino acids: Asp/Glu) at 5, −4, and 3 positions. In addition to O and N amino acids, A amino acids also showed preference with at −2, 10, 3, −1, and −5 positions, in combination with L amino acids at 2 (Figure 2A). 

The presence of aromatic amino acids penultimate or vicinal to the N-glycosylated site supports the N-glycosylation mechanism in the presence of Cyst/Ser/Thr at 2. The P-amino acids, in combination with L at 2, occupied 11 to 13% of positions −3, −9, and 9. Hence, the particular combination of non-polar, polar, aromatic, positive, and negatively charged residues in the vicinity of Asn supports the N-glycosylation process (Figure 2). Although a consensus sequence for N-linked glycosylation (Asn-Xaa-Ser/Thr, where Xaa is not Pro) does exist, this does not guarantee that a protein will undergo this type of modification. To further investigate our findings, we utilized both N-and O-linked web-based glycosylation servers. This freeware examines protein sequences and predicts potentially glycosylated residues based on their surface accessibility, secondary structure and distance constraints. 25,27 The proteins identified by LC-MS/MS were submitted and the results are presented in Table 3. Of the 30 unique proteins identified, 22 contained the signature Asn-Xaa-Ser/Thr motif, with 21 of these proteins identified as positive for N-linked glycosylation sites; 19 proteins contained positive scores for O-linked glycosylation. As shown in Figure 5, only 11 of the proteins identified have been previously reported to be glycosylated (36.67%); our studies resulted in 15 unique and novel glycosylated proteins (50.0%); 4 of these proteins did not fall under either category and are designated "Unreported" (13.33%).
